Root cause: - THORChain_Router tracks does not properly handle rebasing tokens. This is because the system records a static token amount at the time of locking, while the actual token balance may change due to rebasing. - it tracks vault allowances in fragment units, but AMPL rebases change the fragment <-> gons conversion - since allowances don’t rebase while real balances do, a pre‑rebase allowance can later withdraw more gons (value) than intended, draining value from subsequent deposits. - In the case of a positive rebase (balance increases), the user may receive fewer tokens than they are entitled to, resulting in a loss for the user. - In the case of a negative rebase (balance decreases), the system may attempt to transfer more tokens than it actually holds, causing the transaction to revert and funds to become stuck (DoS). PoC: 1. malicious deposits 1000 tokens with _gonsPerFragment == 1, which then executes the following 2 operations: - safeAmount = safeTransferFrom(asset, amount): - tcRouter has 1000 gons (_gonBalances[tcRouter] == 1000) - tcRouter has 1000 balances (_gonsPerFragment == 1) - _vaultAllowance[vault][asset] += safeAmount: malicious has allowance 1000 2. After the rebase, _gonsPerFragment == 2 - tcRouter now has 1000 gons, e.g. 500 balances (_gonsPerFragment == 2) - But malicious still has 1000 allowance 3. victim deposits 1000 tokens with _gonsPerFragment == 2 - safeAmount = safeTransferFrom(asset, amount): - tcRouter has 3000 gons, e.g. 1500 balances (_gonsPerFragment == 2) - _vaultAllowance[vault][asset] += safeAmount: victim has allowance 1000 4. malicious calls transferOut(), which calls ampl.transfer() - tcRouter transfer 2000 gons to malicious (_gonsPerFragment == 2) - tcRouter now has only 1000 gons. e.g. 500 balances - malicious has 2000 gons, e.g. 1000 balances 5. vitim now can only transferOut 500 tokens although it deposits 1000 tokens

Root cause: Router assumes transfer(to, A) delivers A, then instructs the aggregator to act on A. However with Fee-on-Transfer tokens, only A - f arrived, so the aggregator either reverts (tokens get stuck) or pays the shortfall from its own funds (grief/steal). Deep Dive: - In the ERC‑20 path of _transferOutAndCallV5 the Router does two things in sequence: - First deposit the tokens to the aggregator (target) solidity // Router sends `fromAmount` to the aggregator (bool transferSuccess, bytes memory data) = aggregationPayload.fromAsset.call( abi.encodeWithSignature( "transfer(address,uint256)", aggregationPayload.target, aggregationPayload.fromAmount ) ); - Immediately call the aggregator (swapOutV5) with the same fromAmount - However, if the token is fee‑on‑transfer, the aggregator actually receives less in step1, which result in - DoS: If the aggregator has no spare tokens, then swapOutV5 will fail since try to forward fromAmount, but only fromAmount - fee was received. The low-level call returns false, and the router doesn’t revert (by design). Therefore, the tokens remain stuck in the aggregator - grief/steal of aggregator's funds: If the aggregator has spare tokens, it will use its own balance to satisfy fromAmount

The ETH path in _transferOutAndCallV5 re‑uses the same msg.value for every item in the batch, and because the target address is fully attacker‑controlled and unvalidated, the router ends up sending msg.value once per loop iteration, hence drains its own ETH balance. Deep Dive: - The functions transferOutAndCallV5() and batchTransferOutAndCallV5() both internally invoke _transferOutAndCallV5(). This function, in turn, calls the swapOutV5() function on the aggregationPayload.target, which should be the THORChain_Aggregator contract - However, the aggregationPayload is a struct passed as a parameter, which allows anyone to set the aggregationPayload.target address to their preference without any validation. - Even worse, Batch reuses the same msg.value per iteration: - In batchTransferOutAndCallV5, the loop calls _transferOutAndCallV5(aggregationPayloads[i]) N times. - Inside _transferOutAndCallV5, it always sends msg.value to target. There is no decrement and no per‑item value split. - Results in one unit of msg.value leaves the router per iteration—to the attacker’s target or back to msg.sender, which is still attacker
